source.title: Large Language Diffusion Models
source.authors: Shen Nie; Fengqi Zhu; Zebin You; Xiaolu Zhang; Jingyang Ou; Jun Hu; Jun Zhou; Yankai Lin; Ji-Rong Wen; Chong-Xuan Li

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests qualitative downstream-task scaling in a diffusion language model using benchmark scores across pretraining compute, rather than testing held-out cross-entropy power laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports downstream scores across compute levels, which bear on V6. It does not report held-out pretraining loss scaling, fit quantitative curves, or test whether small-run fits predict larger runs. Cited scaling-law results are not extracted as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study trains its own masked-diffusion LMs (LLaDA 1B and 8B) and matched autoregressive baselines. It reports six downstream benchmark scores across pretraining FLOPs (2.2e20 to 8.3e22), which bears on V6 in a new setting (diffusion LMs). It fits no curves and reports no held-out loss, so only the 'improves with scale' part of V6 is tested, not 'predictably'.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that LLaDA scales well on downstream tasks across 1e20 to 1e23 FLOPs and is overall competitive with their ARM baselines, showing stronger scaling on MMLU and GSM8K and a narrowing PIQA gap. They decline to fit curves because of outliers, yet say the results 'clearly demonstrate the scalability of LLaDA'.
record.recipe_differences: The scaling sweep uses masked diffusion models and downstream benchmark scores across pretraining FLOPs, not held-out cross-entropy fits or compute-optimal allocation measurements. ARM baselines are also reported; the models share data, while larger-scale comparisons have some size differences.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that LLaDA's relative performance differs across tasks: its scaling is stronger on MMLU and GSM8K, while the PIQA gap with ARMs narrows as scale increases.
record.problems: The paper does not fit quantitative scaling curves and says it avoids doing so because of possible misinterpretation. The ARM comparison is not fully matched at larger scales: an 8B ARM with the same architecture was not trained, and the reported larger ARM is 7B. The 8B training experiment was run once without hyperparameter tuning; several scaling-table entries are missing because of hardware failures.
record.rows_left_out: Intermediate compute points from Tables 18 and 19 are not extracted; endpoint rows were retained across all six tasks and four reported model variants within the 60-row limit. Those omitted points are relevant to assessing non-monotonicity and curve shape.

untested.parts: Whether improvement is predictable: no curve fits, no extrapolation, no relation to pretraining loss. The authors explicitly decline to fit curves.
No held-out loss or likelihood scaling is reported.
No fitted laws, so no extrapolation test.
No shape ablation at fixed parameter count.
Diffusion LMs are a different training regime, but no power-law form is fitted on any measure.
No exponents or fitting choices are examined.

missing.what: Intermediate compute points showing non-monotone scores. Examples: LLaDA 1B MMLU 35.86 then 31.86; LLaDA 8B HumanEval 12.80 to 6.10; ARM 7B MMLU dipping to 24.41 at 3e21. Needed to judge V6 predictability and curve shape.
The authors' statement that they did not fit quantitative curves because of outliers, which bears on the 'predictably' part of V6.

record.verdict_notes: Comparisons are only partly matched: the 1B models are identical, but the 8B diffusion model is compared with a 7B autoregressive baseline, which was grid-searched while LLaDA was untuned. FLOPs use 6ND with non-embedding parameters. Some GSM8K values are missing due to hardware failure, so R22's value is unreliable. Endpoint-only rows mask the non-monotone curves.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run losses from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
The loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and its trend with compute.
Controlled comparisons of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds in other modalities, repeated-data settings, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The paper reports downstream benchmark scores over compute, but does not fit predictive curves or test prediction from pretraining loss.
Whether scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on fitting choices, or whether loss curves bend from a single power law.

relationships.condition: LLaDA 8B, ARM 7B and ARM 1B sweeps, all six tasks; LLaDA 1B on MMLU, CMMLU, ARC-C and PIQA
relationships.reason: Downstream scores rise substantially from the first to the last compute point, e.g. LLaDA 8B MMLU 32.22 to 58.52 and ARM 7B GSM8K 1.29 to 27.37. This is qualitative only (R01–R08, R13–R21, R23–R48).
relationships.display_finding: Scores increased substantially between the first and last compute settings, including LLaDA 8B MMLU from 32.22 to 58.52 and ARM 7B GSM8K from 1.29 to 27.37.

relationships.condition: LLaDA 1B on GSM8K and HumanEval (near-floor tasks at small compute); non-monotone intermediate points
relationships.reason: GSM8K (1.82 to 2.35) and HumanEval (0 to 0.61) barely move (R09–R12). Intermediate points in Tables 18 and 19 dip, and the authors avoid fitting curves because of outliers. Predictability is therefore not shown.
relationships.display_finding: GSM8K rose only from 1.82 to 2.35 and HumanEval from 0 to 0.61, with intermediate declines and outliers preventing curve fitting.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: Endpoint comparisons across the reported LLaDA and ARM pretraining-compute sweeps, on the six evaluated tasks
reader_labels.reason: Scores rise from the first to last listed compute point for each represented model and task; these results support qualitative downstream scaling, but not quantitative prediction (R01–R48).
